title: Easy exam 10
about: Ten single-choice questions on the basics: find by group, xargs, comparing files, case, df and du, line editing, root's powers, echo escapes, passwd and pstree.

questions.title: find by group
questions.text: In `/srv` there are regular files and directories that belong to the group `devs`, and files of other groups. What does `find /srv -group devs -type f` print?

options.t: The paths of the regular files whose group is `devs`.
options.why: `-group` selects by group and `-type f` keeps only regular files; both tests must be true.

options.t: The paths of every entry of the group `devs`, directories included.
options.why: `-type f` removes the directories from the result.

options.t: The paths of the files that are owned by the user `devs`.
options.why: `-group` looks at the group; the owner is tested with `-user`.

options.t: The paths of the files that members of `devs` are allowed to write.
options.why: `find` does not test what the group may do, only who the owner group is (that would be `-perm`).

questions.title: Names that arrive on stdin
questions.text: `trash.txt` contains the names of two files, one per line. Which command deletes those two files?

options.t: `xargs rm < trash.txt`
options.why: `xargs` reads the names from its input and runs `rm` with them as arguments.

options.t: `rm < trash.txt`
options.why: `rm` does not read its standard input: it complains "missing operand".

options.t: `cat trash.txt | rm`
options.why: Through the pipe the names arrive on stdin, which `rm` ignores: "missing operand".

options.t: `rm -f < trash.txt`
options.why: `-f` only silences errors about missing files; the input is still ignored.

questions.title: Comparing byte by byte
questions.text: Which command compares two files byte by byte and reports the position of the first difference?

options.t: `cmp`
options.why: For example `cmp f1 f2` prints `f1 f2 differ: byte 3, line 1`.

options.t: `diff`
options.why: It compares line by line and lists the lines that changed, not byte positions.

options.t: `od`
options.why: It dumps the content of one file in octal, hexadecimal or characters; it compares nothing.

options.t: `wc -c`
options.why: It counts the bytes of a file; it cannot tell where two files differ.

questions.title: case patterns
questions.text: Which statement about the `case` command is FALSE?

options.t: A `case` ends with `esac`.
options.why: True: it is `case` written backwards, as `fi` closes an `if`.

options.t: Each branch ends with `;;`.
options.why: True: the double semicolon closes the commands of the branch.

options.t: The pattern `*)` matches anything, so it is used as the default branch.
options.why: True: patterns are tried in order and the first match wins.

options.t: The patterns are regular expressions, so `a.c)` matches `abc`.
options.why: False: the patterns are shell globs. There `.` is an ordinary character, so `a.c` matches only the text `a.c`.

options.t: `df` reports the space of each mounted file system; `du` adds up the space used by a directory tree.
options.why: Typical uses: `df -h` to see how full the disks are and `du -sh dir` to see how big a directory is.

options.t: `df` adds up the space used by a directory tree and `du` reports the free space of each mounted file system.
options.why: It is the other way round.

options.t: Both print the free space of the disk; `du` is just the old name of `df`.
options.why: They are different commands that answer different questions.

options.t: `df -h` shows the size of every file in the current directory.
options.why: `df` works with file systems, not with individual files.

questions.title: Editing the command line
questions.text: Which statement about editing and recalling commands in the shell is FALSE?

options.t: `Tab` completes the name of a command or file as far as it is unambiguous.
options.why: True: pressed twice it lists the possibilities.

options.t: `Ctrl+A` moves the cursor to the beginning of the line and `Ctrl+E` to the end.
options.why: True: they are the Emacs-style keys of the line editor.

options.t: The command `history` prints the numbered list of the commands typed before.
options.why: True: `!N` repeats the one with number N.

options.t: The up arrow recalls the previous command and runs it at once, without waiting for Enter.
options.why: False: it only puts the command on the line so that you can edit it; it runs when you press Enter.

questions.title: root and permissions
questions.text: The file `secret` belongs to `ana` and has mode `000`. Logged in as `root`, you run `cat secret`. What happens?

options.t: The content is printed.
options.why: root bypasses the read and write permission checks; only execute needs at least one `x` bit.

options.t: "Permission denied", because nobody has read permission.
options.why: The permission checks do not apply to root.

options.t: "Permission denied", because root is not the owner.
options.why: Being the owner is not required for root.

options.t: It prints the content only after `chmod +r secret`, since even root needs read permission.
options.why: root does not need to change the mode first.

questions.title: The -e option of echo
questions.text: Which option makes `echo` interpret escape sequences such as `\n` and `\t`?

options.why: `echo -e "a\tb"` prints `a`, a tab and `b`.
It only suppresses the final newline.
It disables the interpretation of escapes, which is already the default in bash.
`echo` has no such option: it just prints `-s` as text.

questions.title: Locking an account
questions.text: Which command locks the password of the user `ana`, so that she cannot log in with it?

options.t: `passwd -l ana`
options.why: `-l` (lock) disables the password; `-u` undoes it.

options.t: `passwd -u ana`
options.why: `-u` unlocks the password.

options.t: `passwd -e ana`
options.why: `-e` expires the password: it stays valid, but she must change it at the next login.

options.t: `passwd -d ana`
options.why: `-d` deletes the password, leaving the account with no password at all: the opposite of what is wanted.

options.t: It shows the processes as a tree: each child under its parent, PID 1 at the root.
options.why: With `pstree -p` the PIDs are shown next to the names.

options.t: It shows only the processes of the current user, as a flat table with one column per attribute.
options.why: A flat table of columns is what `ps` prints.

options.t: It draws the tree of directories of the file system.
options.why: That is what `tree` does.

options.t: It orders the processes by memory usage.
options.why: Sorting by memory is done inside `top` or with `ps --sort`.
